title: Responses API parity: stateful session routing, streaming loss analysis, and mapping heuristics
creator: Marisol Vega
description:
Goal: implement a lightweight compatibility layer that maps Redwood request/response shapes to OpenAI Responses semantics while preserving stateful session routing, minimizing streaming loss, and maintaining fidelity for function/tool calls and structured outputs. This ticket covers the discovery, mapping heuristics, and mitigations for observed feature parity gaps (not the full adapter implementation).

Scope:
- Catalog concrete behavioral deltas between Redwood runtime and OpenAI Responses for ongoing conversations and streaming events.
- Define mapping heuristics for session identifiers, KV cache interaction, and event chunk reconstruction.
- Prototype loss-detection telemetry and a degradation strategy that preserves function call ordering and structured output integrity.
- Deliver unit/integration test matrix and canary rollout checklist.

Key parity gaps identified so far (summary):
1) Streaming event boundary differences: Responses service may emit partial JSON fragments split across chunks or combine multiple logical events into one packet; runtime reassembly currently assumes per-event framing.
2) Session identity and conversation continuity: OpenAI Responses relies on ephemeral conversation ids and implicit session affinity; Redwood's routing can reshard or move sessions across workers which breaks in-flight KV cache assumptions.
3) Function/tool call ordering and metadata: Responses exposes toolcall metadata inline with text deltas; Redwood's tool routing expects discrete tool-call events. Ordering mismatches lead to duplicate invocations or dropped tool calls.
4) Structured output typing and strictness: Responses may include nullable/absent fields or type variants (string vs object) for the same schema; Redwood SDK consumers expect consistent typed objects.
5) Token provenance and attribution: Differences in tokenization boundaries and provenance fields between platforms cause audit and cost-reporting mismatches.

Non-goals: full adapter implementation for all models, or solving server-side kernel scheduling. Focus is on mapping rules, tests, and short-term mitigations that enable predictable degradation for customers during migration/canary flow.
proposed_implementation: Create a mapping layer module (responses_mapper) with pluggable heuristics: chunk_reassembler, session_affinity_guard, toolcall_normalizer, structured_output_normalizer.

Implement a streaming reassembler that uses heuristic boundaries (bracket/JSON-balanced detection + length headers when present) and emits 'reassembly warnings' for telemetry when heuristics are used.

Session affinity guard: add a lightweight sticky-routing token for compatibility proxy requests to keep KV cache pinned for session hot-paths; fall back to 'stateless' mode with a strong warning when affinity cannot be maintained.
Toolcall normalizer: buffer tool-call related events until a stable ordering is observed (bounded buffer with timeout), attach synthetic ids to ensure idempotency on retries.

Structured output normalizer: apply tolerant decoding (accept multiple types) and run schema coercion rules to preserve shape expected by SDKs; emit field-mismatch telemetry for later strictness policy.
Telemetry: add loss_score, reassembly_used, affinity_broken, toolcall_reordered metrics to runtime tracing and to the per-request diagnostic payload stored in the console for canary customers.

Testing: unit tests for chunk_reassembler with fuzzed chunk boundaries, integration test that runs against a Responses v2 stub that emits known edge cases, and a canary plan with synthetic workloads (chat streaming + function calls + structured response).
acceptance_criteria: Mapping module checked into repo with feature-flag guarded activation.
Streaming reassembler passes deterministic fuzz harness (>=98% reassembly success on synthetic corpus of edge cases).
Toolcall normalizer preserves call-order and deduplicates retries in 99% of simulated multi-worker reorders within bounded buffer window.
Structured outputs normalized such that SDK-level schema conversion tests pass (no TypeErrors in consumer harness).
Telemetry fields appear in Console for enabled canary orgs and alert when loss_score > threshold.
Canary rollout playbook documented with rollback hooks and links to dashboards.

2026-03-05 - Spike complete: prototype reassembler shows promise but fails on nested JSON arrays split across 3 chunks. Recorded sample messages to /drive/responses_reassembly/samples.zip.

2026-03-08 - Design review with UX/SDK (Rohit, Lina, Priya): agreed to emit 'reassembly warnings' and not to silently mutate top-level ids. Decided to implement bounded buffering for toolcalls (250ms or 4 events).
2026-03-10 - Security review preliminary: no secrets persisted; affinity token will be short-lived and scoped to request. Security asked for KMS audit in telemetry path; ticket created ENG-802345.

2026-03-12 - Implemented initial chunk_reassembler in branch feat/responses-mapper; pushed draft PR to GitHub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4128. Tests currently failing on specific nested-array fragmentation case.
2026-03-14 - Work in progress: fixing edge-case handling and adding more fuzz cases. Planned pairing session with SDK team next week to validate schema coercions.
notes: Trade-offs considered: stronger strictness (reject mismatched types) vs. permissive normalization (best-effort coercion). We chose permissive normalization for canary release to reduce customer impact, with plan to tighten after 2 weeks of telemetry. Affinity tokens introduce operational complexity but are the least invasive way to preserve KV cache continuity without large routing changes. Buffering toolcalls increases end-to-end latency slightly; bounded 250ms chosen as compromise.
